added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: a new paradigm is established and then all of a sudden people hop over from the old paradigm to the new paradigm without kind of explaining why they made the jump.
added_claims.claim: Allocation paradigm shifts (Kuhn's structure of scientific revolutions) happen abruptly rather than gradually: once the 60/40 playbook broke, wealth managers jump to a new framework (stocks, shrinking bonds, plus an 'other' diversifier bucket) without explaining the break, which is what opens the door for managed futures and other alternatives.
added_claims.direction: flows move from bonds to diversifying alternatives
added_claims.conditions: after a long-standing portfolio rule visibly fails (bonds not diversifying in this decade)
added_claims.testable: partly - fund-flow data into alternatives after 2022

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: some short-term managers uh have had real challenges in November, which um the surface numbers don't really um explain.
added_claims.claim: In November 2025 short-term trend managers struggled even though the headline trend indices looked flat, so aggregate index moves can hide dispersion between short-term and longer-term models.
added_claims.indicator: short-term CTA performance versus trend index
added_claims.testable: yes - compare SG Short-Term Traders Index with SG Trend Index monthly

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: we rebalance on Mondays. Sometimes it feels like a great decision. Sometimes you know you you really wish you'd rebalance the prior Thursday or the next Tuesday or something.
added_claims.claim: A third source of divergence from the CTA index is pure timing noise: a fixed weekly rebalance day sometimes gains and sometimes loses a few days of signal drift relative to peers, so some relative performance is luck rather than design.
added_claims.testable: yes - shift the rebalance weekday and measure P&L dispersion

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: We don't know the answer to that, and we're actually not going to know the answer to that for a few years.
added_claims.claim: Whether the extras that most CTAs add (short-term models, vol controls, exotic markets) destroy value relative to a 10-market major-market signal is not yet known and will take several more years of live evidence to resolve; the 2024-2025 outperformance is suggestive, not conclusive.
added_claims.conditions: needs several more years of live data across regimes
added_claims.testable: yes - out-of-sample comparison of 10-market versus wide-universe CTA indices

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: we can create an index on Monday if it's not working by Thursday we'll shut it down we'll launch a new one the following Monday
added_claims.claim: Derivative-based strategy indices can be created overnight and closed or replaced if they fail, so a bank-published index with a backfilled history carries survivorship and selection bias unless the rules were fixed and live before the history was shown.
added_claims.conditions: applies to rules-based swap/derivative indices launched by banks
added_claims.testable: yes - compare backfilled index performance with performance after launch

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: by 2024, having now proven year after year after year after year this rep replication strategy worked without changing it, we then could launch an index around it.
added_claims.claim: Allocators are rightly sceptical of hypothetical backtests, so credibility for an index comes from running the identical rules live for years without changes before building a benchmark on them.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare rule stability and live versus backtest returns

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they only trade two of the four different asset classes they're up 24% or something in 2024 I mean it's very very different return profile
added_claims.claim: Simplify's existing CTA ETF is a different product from the DBMF-style replication (it trades only two of four asset classes and had a very different return profile, up about 24% in 2024), so the same label covers materially different exposures.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare return series and asset-class exposures

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: I believe that there is a lot more flexibility on the structuring side that can also solve things on the tax side for people
added_claims.claim: Accessing a strategy through swaps or derivatives on an index allows structuring flexibility (notes, principal protection, excess-return versions) that can improve tax efficiency, so tax effectiveness should be counted alongside fees when comparing implementations.
added_claims.conditions: depends on investor tax status and vehicle
added_claims.testable: partly - after-tax return comparison of swap, ETF and fund wrappers

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: studying historical prices which academics tell us it shouldn't work. Why? It's worked for 50 years, right?
added_claims.claim: Trend following using only historical prices has worked for about 50 years despite academic weak-form efficiency arguments, and its profits come from institutions with slow, fixed models rather than from other trend followers.
added_claims.testable: yes - long-run trend index returns net of costs

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: small changes in assumptions around implementation costs or speed or things like that can have an
added_claims.claim: CTA design choices are highly sensitive to small changes in assumed implementation costs or signal speed, which is why equally smart managers reach opposite conclusions on the same data; the heterogeneity of approaches across the space is therefore a healthy feature.
added_claims.testable: yes - sensitivity analysis of net returns to cost and speed assumptions

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they'll take four of the six or four of the eight people in the room and put them together into a portfolio to try to cancel out a lot of these differences
added_claims.claim: Because allocators cannot yet get the core trend signal efficiently, they bolt together several managers to average out differences, ending up with an index-like blend of 'beta adjacent' strategies that is inefficient compared with owning the core directly and adding satellites.
added_claims.conditions: holds if a cheap, efficient core trend allocation is available
added_claims.testable: yes - compare a multi-manager blend with a core-plus-satellite portfolio on net Sharpe and fees

corrections.issue: Attributes the full ~500bp of post-Liberation-Day outperformance to slower de-risking. The speaker says the 500bp arose in the days after Liberation Day mostly because the major-market-only portfolio was less whipsawed than portfolios with esoteric markets; slower de-risking is a separate second factor that added only 'a couple of points' when Trump changed course.
corrections.fix: A replication fund with a short-but-not-very-short lookback was a little slower to de-risk in April 2025, and when the tariff shock reversed it still held residual risk, adding roughly two points of return; the larger ~500bp outperformance in the days after Liberation Day came mainly from holding only 10 major markets (see C05-1).

corrections.issue: The caption is garbled and the first-reader claim treats '100bp performance differential in the ETF' as one of three additive reasons; the speaker also says the 150bp is what is not explained by the management-fee difference, which suggests the first ~100bp is a fee/cost difference and that part of the gap may just be higher volatility in a rising market.
corrections.fix: Beer says the ETF beats the multi-manager Abbey Capital by about 350bp over time: about 100bp from a cost/performance differential in the ETF, some from taking somewhat more volatility in a rising market, and at least another ~150bp that the management-fee difference does not explain. Low confidence because the transcript caption is unclear.

completeness_estimate: 0.85 - the first reader caught the main replication, cost-debate, crystal-ball and alpha/beta arguments with correct numbers; it missed research-method points (index survivorship, hypothetical-number scepticism, timing noise, sensitivity of design to cost assumptions), tax structuring and the allocator manager-blending point, and slightly overstated the effect of slow de-risking.
